title: Pre-Encryption Encoding for Post-Quantum IoT Messaging with ML-KEM: Comparing Static, Huffman, and Compression-Based Schemes
content: Post-quantum messaging with ML-KEM (FIPS 203) fixes its asymmetric cost at one encapsulation per session, so the remaining lever for constrained devices is how plaintext is represented before symmetric encryption. A recent study favored a 6-bit static code over Huffman coding for Kyber, measuring outside the KEM-DEM construction and charging only Huffman coding for its table; we repeat the comparison inside a standardized ML-KEM-512, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM pipeline with pre-shared state granted to every scheme. Seven encodings — the static code, pre-shared Huffman coding, zstd with and without a dictionary, the microcontroller-class heatshrink and Unishox2, and UTF-8 — are measured on prose, chat, uniform, and synthetic and real sensor-telemetry corpora of 120–20,000 characters, all timed in C on five input slices. Encoding cuts payload by up to 56% on text and 51–61% on 120-character sensor messages, saving whole LoRaWAN frames, while the 768-byte ML-KEM ciphertext alone needs 16 frames at SF12. A 2 KB dictionary beats pre-shared Huffman coding from 500 characters on non-uniform data, but Huffman coding keeps 120-character real sensor messages. The static code’s decode advantage is 5–14× against a bit-serial Huffman decoder but 3–5× against a table-driven one. Code and data are released.
